blocks.text: Streaming APIs deliver a generated response incrementally, token by token, as the model actually produces it, rather than waiting for the complete response the way the synchronous pattern covered in the earlier API Architecture topic does, this closing topic covers how LLM providers commonly implement this over standard HTTP.

This topic covers server-sent events as the common streaming mechanism, why streaming improves perceived latency, parsing a streaming response in application code, and how streaming here differs from the full WebSocket protocol covered in a related topic.
1. What Streaming Means for an LLM Response

blocks.alt: Building on REST APIs, streaming APIs deliver incremental token delivery

blocks.text: A streaming API response delivers generated content incrementally, sending each piece of text as the model actually produces it, rather than waiting until generation completes entirely before sending anything back at all.
2. Synchronous vs Streaming, Revisited

blocks.alt: A synchronous response waits for the complete output, streaming delivers tokens incrementally

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the earlier API Architecture topic, which introduced this distinction, a synchronous call returns nothing until the model has finished generating the entire response, streaming returns content as it becomes available, this topic covers the actual mechanics behind that streaming option.
3. Server-Sent Events as the Common Mechanism

blocks.alt: An HTTP connection stays open, using the server-sent events format, sending chunks as they are generated

blocks.text: This connects directly to the REST APIs topic covered earlier in this module, LLM providers commonly implement streaming by keeping a standard HTTP connection open and sending a sequence of small data chunks using the server-sent events format, a simpler, one directional streaming mechanism built directly on top of ordinary HTTP.
4. Token-by-Token Delivery

blocks.alt: A token arrives, then the next token arrives, then the next

blocks.text: This connects directly to the earlier How LLMs Process Prompts topic, since the model genuinely generates output one token at a time, streaming naturally maps to sending each newly generated token, or small group of tokens, to the client as soon as it exists, rather than artificially buffering the entire response.
5. Why Streaming Improves Perceived Latency

blocks.alt: A user waiting for the full response is compared against a user seeing text appear progressively

blocks.text: Streaming does not actually make the model generate faster, the total generation time is the same, but a user seeing text appear progressively, word by word, perceives the experience as meaningfully faster and more responsive than staring at a blank screen until the entire response is ready.

blocks.text: 6. Parsing a Streaming Response in Application Code

blocks.alt: An application parses each incoming chunk and appends it to the displayed text

blocks.text: An application consuming a streaming response reads incoming chunks as they arrive, parses each one, and appends the new content to whatever is already displayed to the user, this requires genuinely different application code than handling a single synchronous response received all at once.

blocks.title: Most SDKs handle this parsing complexity for you
blocks.content: This connects directly to SDKs, covered earlier in this module, most official provider SDKs expose a simple iteration interface over a streaming response, handling the underlying chunk parsing internally so your application code can focus on what to do with each piece of new content.

blocks.text: 7. Streaming Here vs Full WebSockets

blocks.alt: Streaming here is one way over standard HTTP, WebSockets provide a full bidirectional persistent connection

blocks.text: This is worth distinguishing clearly, the streaming covered in this topic is typically one directional, the server sends chunks to the client over a standard HTTP connection kept open, a full WebSocket connection, covered in its own dedicated topic, provides genuine two-way, persistent communication, useful for scenarios needing the client to also send data back mid-stream, most LLM chat completion streaming does not actually need that full bidirectional capability.
8. Handling a Connection That Drops Mid-Response

A streaming connection can drop partway through generation, due to a network issue or timeout, a well built application detects this and handles it explicitly, showing a partial response with an indication it was interrupted, or offering to retry, rather than leaving a user staring at an response that silently stopped with no explanation.
9. This Module Is Now Complete

This closes out the LLM APIs Fundamentals module, what an LLM API is, API architecture, authentication, API keys, rate limiting, quotas, SDKs, REST APIs, and now streaming APIs, together forming the foundational mechanics every provider specific module later in this course builds directly on.
Worked Example

A team building a chat interface initially uses only synchronous API calls, user feedback consistently describes the experience as feeling slow, even though the actual total response time is reasonable.

Switching to a streaming implementation, displaying each token as it arrives rather than waiting for the complete response, produces no change in actual total generation time, but user perception of speed improves dramatically, demonstrating why streaming matters for user experience even when it does not change the underlying computation time at all.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming streaming makes generation faster rather than just changing how progressively the result becomes visible
Not handling a dropped streaming connection explicitly, leaving a user confused by a silently incomplete response
Confusing this one directional HTTP streaming pattern with a full, bidirectional WebSocket connection
Writing custom streaming chunk parsing logic when the provider SDK already handles this reliably

blocks.text: Practice

Take an application feature you have built or could build using a synchronous API call, sketch out what would need to change to support streaming instead, how the application would consume and display incoming chunks, and consider whether the user experience would genuinely benefit from that change.
Key Takeaway

Streaming APIs deliver generated content incrementally as the model produces it, commonly through server-sent events over a standard HTTP connection, genuinely improving perceived latency even though total generation time stays the same, and it is a simpler, typically one directional pattern distinct from the full bidirectional communication a genuine WebSocket connection provides.
